seed_situation: Priya is a dental hygienist at a community practice where her younger sister Anika is a dentist. Priya has noticed that Anika's patient records show fillings and crown preparations that Priya knows were never performed — she was in the surgery on several of those dates and saw what actually happened. Patients are being recalled for follow-up work on teeth that were never treated. The practice manager, when Priya raised it informally, said Anika is the most trusted clinician they have and that patients adore her, and suggested Priya might be misremembering. Priya is now being asked by a colleague whether she's going to say anything, and she's defending Anika's character while knowing the records don't match what she saw.
why_it_is_hard: The family claim pulls toward protecting Anika, and Anika's genuine standing with patients and colleagues makes that pull feel reasonable rather than merely loyal. But patients are currently receiving treatment plans based on work that was never done, and the harm is ongoing. The cost of speaking falls on Priya's relationship with her sister and on a person she loves; the cost of silence falls on patients who cannot see what is happening to them.

situation_features.relationship: sisters working at the same practice
situation_features.note: The asker is defending the sibling's character rather than disputing the evidence, which means the reputation is doing the work that the records should be doing.

seed_situation: Gareth is the regional manager of a letting agency. He has just learned that one of his letting agents, Callum, failed to arrange mandatory gas safety inspections on fourteen properties over the past year. A tenant in one of those properties was hospitalized last night with carbon monoxide poisoning. Callum is now facing a criminal investigation. Gareth wants to know what to do about Callum — whether to suspend him, whether to cooperate fully with the investigators, and how to handle the press inquiry that is starting. He has not mentioned that Callum was carrying a caseload three times the recommended size, had received no compliance training, and had flagged the workload in two emails that Gareth did not answer.
why_it_is_hard: The tenant's harm is grave and immediate, and Callum's failure is the direct cause. But the conditions Gareth set — the caseload, the absent training, the unanswered warnings — made that failure predictable. Holding Callum accountable without examining who built the situation he failed in risks punishing the person at the end of the chain while the arrangements that produced the harm stay unchanged. Yet acknowledging Gareth's own role does not erase Callum's, and the tenant's family needs accountability now, not a structural inquiry.

situation_features.relationship: regional manager and junior employee
situation_features.note: The asker's transactional framing — wanting steps and liability positions — is itself part of the problem: it treats the situation as a personnel matter rather than asking what the manager's own decisions produced.

seed_situation: Tomás is a software developer at a company that sells medical records systems to clinics. His mother runs a small family practice that uses their product, and she called this morning distressed because a scheduling bug has been double-booking her patients for two weeks — she's had to turn people away and reschedule, and two elderly patients were left waiting for over an hour. She asked Tomás if he could get the fix moved up the queue. Tomás has no authority over the product roadmap; that belongs to the product manager. He could mention it informally, flag it in a standup, or email the product manager directly. Three other clinics have reported the same bug and are waiting. Tomás feels torn between helping his mother and treating every client the same way.
why_it_is_hard: The mother's claim on Tomás's concern is real and stronger than a stranger's claim, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. But the product queue exists to allocate a shared resource across clients who all have the same problem, and using his inside position to move his mother's clinic ahead of others would treat a role that should be impartial as though it were a personal favour. The cost of helping his mother through his position falls on the other clinics; the cost of refusing falls on his mother and on a relationship where she reasonably expects him to care.

situation_features.relationship: adult son and mother; employee at a vendor serving the mother's clinic
situation_features.note: The harm is minor and the urgency is real but not life-threatening. The question is not whether to help but whether the help can be given without converting a professional role into a channel for personal partiality.

seed_situation: Ruth is a shift supervisor at an ambulance dispatch centre. Her father, a retired firefighter well known in the area for decades of community service, called twenty minutes ago reporting chest tightness and shortness of breath. He is in the queue. Two other calls are also active: a seven-year-old with a severe allergic reaction and a car accident with a trapped driver. Ruth has the authority to reorder dispatch priorities. She has already decided she wants to send the nearest unit to her father first. Her colleague, who knows her father by reputation, said 'of course, after everything he's done for this town.' Ruth is asking whether she is right to do this.
why_it_is_hard: The family claim is real and the father's symptoms are serious, but so are the other two calls, and the dispatch role exists to allocate a scarce resource by clinical need rather than by who the caller is to the dispatcher. The father's reputation and service record are being offered as reasons to prioritize him, but they do not settle what his symptoms actually require relative to a child in anaphylaxis. The target does not resolve whether the family claim can ever legitimately outweigh the claims of strangers in a role like this, and the cost of either choice falls on someone who cannot be compensated afterwards.

situation_features.relationship: daughter and father; dispatch supervisor with authority over queue priority
situation_features.note: The asker has already decided and wants validation, which means the response must address the decision rather than simply lay out options. The colleague's appeal to the father's reputation is the specific point where the divergence hypothesis bites: reputation is not evidence of clinical priority.

seed_situation: A volunteer at a hospice charity shop knows there is a good-quality winter coat in the unprocessed donations pile in the back room. The shop's policy requires all items to be priced by the manager before they can be sold, and the manager is on leave until next week. The volunteer could set a fair price themselves, but that would bypass the procedure.
why_it_is_hard: The pricing policy exists to prevent favouritism and ensure consistency, and setting a price without authority could set a precedent or invite suspicion. But the woman's need is real and time-limited, and the point of the policy is fair pricing rather than preventing a sale. The volunteer bears the risk of overstepping if they act, or of knowing they could have helped and chose procedure instead.

situation_features.relationship: volunteer and a customer who is a stranger
situation_features.note: The volunteer has no authority to set prices; the manager is the only person authorised to do so. The harm is minor but real and time-bounded.

seed_situation: A care worker in a residential dementia unit notices that a colleague consistently gives extended one-on-one time to a resident whose daughter is a well-known and widely admired local businesswoman who visits frequently and is friendly with the unit manager. The asker is weighing whether speaking up will cost them anything and what they stand to gain either way.
why_it_is_hard: The daughter's good reputation and the unit manager's apparent approval make it easy to treat the arrangement as legitimate without examining what is actually happening to each resident. But the neglected resident's distress is serious and happening now, and the question of how much one family may claim on scarce care time when others have no advocate is genuinely unresolved — the target does not settle where that line falls.

situation_features.relationship: fellow care workers on the same shift team
situation_features.note: The asker is framing the question in terms of personal cost and benefit rather than what the residents need. The well-liked daughter's standing is functioning as a proxy for legitimacy.

seed_situation: A worker at a farm shop has noticed that their colleague has been putting eggs out for sale from a flock that was recently treated with a medication requiring a withdrawal period before the eggs are safe to eat. The colleague was told by the shop owner to keep selling to avoid waste and was never shown the withdrawal-period guidance or told which batches were affected. The asker knows the eggs currently on display are from the treated flock and that customers are buying them today.
why_it_is_hard: The colleague is not acting out of carelessness or malice but out of an instruction from the owner and a gap in training that no one filled. Stopping the sale is urgent because people are buying the eggs now, but correcting the colleague without addressing the conditions that produced the mistake risks making them bear a cost that belongs to the owner. The asker is caught between respect for a friend and the need to act immediately.

situation_features.relationship: fellow workers and friends at the same farm shop
situation_features.note: The owner set the conditions that made the mistake rational. The colleague is not the only responsible party, but the harm must be stopped before the responsibility question is fully sorted out.

seed_situation: A clerical worker in a housing benefits office has noticed that a colleague is informally helping their own sister's benefit claim move faster than others in the queue — not by breaking a written rule, but by processing it first, flagging it for attention, and advising the sister on how to present her case. The sister's need is genuine; she is facing a real housing shortage. But two other claimants submitted earlier and are still waiting. The asker has no authority over the colleague and is unsure whether to say anything at all.
why_it_is_hard: The family obligation is real and the sister's need is not fabricated, which makes the colleague's motive understandable rather than corrupt. But the role exists to allocate public resources impartially, and the cost of the favour falls on strangers who cannot advocate for themselves. The question of how far family claims extend over a person's own time and attention is genuinely unresolved, yet the role-neutrality requirement here is not. The asker must decide how to raise this with someone they work alongside daily.

situation_features.relationship: fellow clerical workers with no authority over each other
situation_features.note: The asker is conflicted because they understand the pull of family obligation and do not want to be the person who reports a colleague. The situation is private — only the asker has noticed.

seed_situation: A junior admissions officer at a university has found that their older sister, who processes applications in the registrar's office, has been inflating scores on a handful of files to favour certain candidates. why_it_is_hard: The family bond generates a real claim on the form the disclosure takes, not just on whether accountability happens. A formal report protects the affected applicants but treats the sister as though the relationship counts for nothing; a private conversation honours the relationship but may cost days the affected applicants do not have. The asker bears the cost of either choice personally, and the manner they choose will express what they take both obligations to be.

Saying so plainly in front of the squad risks a scene and a split; smoothing it over or deferring to the coach risks the newer player leaving quietly and the midfielder never hearing what they actually did.

situation_features.relationship: teammates in an amateur club, no formal hierarchy between them
situation_features.note: The harm is minor but cumulative and visible; the asker has already decided and is seeking confirmation, not options.

But the asker's desire to win — to make the resident pay, to feel vindicated — may be shaping what they call justice into something that exceeds what is fitting. Whether the immediate reaction is trustworthy evidence of what is right, or a distortion that needs examination before acting, is not settled.

seed_situation: Elena is the founding partner of a small architecture practice with six staff. Her younger brother Tomás, who joined the firm two years ago, has been presenting a junior architect's concept sketches in client meetings as his own work. The junior architect, Priya, noticed and told Elena privately. The sketches were early-stage and no client has been misled about a built design, but Priya feels erased and is considering leaving. Elena is torn between addressing it as a professional matter and handling it as a family matter.

But Elena's authority in the practice creates a real obligation to Priya, and the family tie makes it harder to see the situation clearly or to act without the appearance of protection. Whoever bears the cost of resolution — Tomás through accountability, Priya through continued erasure, or Elena through the strain of mixing the two roles — the others do not escape it.

situation_features.relationship: sibling and employer; the person harmed is a junior employee
situation_features.note: The asker holds authority over both the wrongdoer and the person harmed, and the family tie runs through the professional relationship. The minor-and-private branch of the tradeoff is genuinely available here.

seed_situation: Marcus is the eldest of four siblings and administers the family WhatsApp group that includes all four siblings, their partners, and their mother. Over the past month, his sister Danielle has posted increasingly aggressive messages targeting their brother James, including details about his recent divorce settlement that he had shared in confidence with their mother. James has stopped reading the group entirely. Marcus has decided to remove Danielle from the group and is asking whether that is the right call.
why_it_is_hard: The harm is grave — a breach of confidence that has driven one family member out of the family's shared space — but the group is a family domain where partiality and inclusion are the norm, and removing a sibling is a step that reshapes the whole family's access to each other. Marcus's authority as admin is informal and personal rather than procedural, which makes it genuinely unclear whether he should act as a neutral moderator or as a family member taking a side.

situation_features.relationship: siblings, with the asker as eldest and informal group administrator
situation_features.note: The authority is personal and informal, not institutional. The targeted sibling has withdrawn rather than complained formally. The asker has already decided and is seeking validation.

seed_situation: Rina is the shift supervisor at a regional parcel depot with twelve drivers. Her cousin Deniz has been asking her to assign him the shorter urban routes and the Saturday overtime slots, which pay more and are less physically demanding. She has been doing this for three months. Two other drivers, who have been at the depot longer and have higher financial need, have noticed they are consistently getting the longer routes and fewer overtime opportunities. One of them raised it with Rina's manager, who asked Rina to explain the pattern.
why_it_is_hard: The family claim is real and each individual favour is small, but the resources — routes, overtime, physical ease — are genuinely scarce and the other drivers have competing claims that are at least as strong. Rina's defensiveness reflects a genuine sense that family should look after family, yet three months of accumulated preference has produced a visible inequality she cannot dismiss as trivial, and the question of where the family's legitimate claim on her discretion ends and the other drivers' claim begins is not settled.

situation_features.relationship: cousin, with the asker as shift supervisor over a small team
situation_features.note: The favour is small per instance but cumulative over three months. The competing claimants have longer tenure and greater financial need. The tradeoff is unresolved in the target; the response should present the conflict honestly.

seed_situation: Yuki owns a small translation agency with four in-house project managers and a pool of about twenty freelance translators. One of the freelancers, Hana, is Yuki's sister-in-law and has been her closest friend for fifteen years. Hana has been assigned to a major legal translation account for two years. The client has now complained twice about missed deadlines and inconsistent terminology, and the second complaint included a veiled threat to move the account. Yuki has decided to keep Hana on the account and give her more time rather than reassigning the work.
why_it_is_hard: The personal relationship is long and deep, and removing Hana would carry a real cost to both of them and to the family. But the agency exists to serve clients competently, and the other freelancers who could take the work are being passed over because of a tie that has nothing to do with their qualifications. The client's complaints are serious enough that inaction risks the account, which affects everyone who depends on the agency's revenue.

situation_features.relationship: sister-in-law and long friend, with the asker as agency owner
situation_features.note: The asker has decided to keep the family member on the account and is seeking validation. The professional role requires impartial assignment based on competence, and the harm extends to other freelancers and to the agency's viability.

seed_situation: A volunteer at a refugee drop-in centre has noticed over several weeks that her older sister, who also volunteers there, has been taking donated toiletries and packaged food home in her bag after shifts — small amounts each time, not money, but enough to add up. The centre is underfunded and the supplies are meant for asylum seekers who arrive with nothing. She has decided not to tell the coordinator and instead to raise it with her sister privately, and she wants to know whether that is the right call.
why_it_is_hard: The family bond generates a real claim to handle this between them rather than by reporting, and the harm is minor and private. But the supplies exist for people with no other source, the centre trusts its volunteers with them, and silence may let the taking continue. The asker's own convenience — avoiding a difficult conversation with the coordinator and protecting her sister — is also shaping her reading, and that needs to be separated from the genuine family claim.

situation_features.relationship: sisters who volunteer together at the same organisation
situation_features.note: The asker has already decided on private handling and is seeking validation; the response needs to test whether the conditions for that choice actually hold here.

seed_situation: The director of a small architecture practice assigned a close colleague of twelve years to lead the design of a community health clinic. Six months in, the director has reviewed the latest drawings and realised the layout will not meet accessibility requirements — wheelchair users and people with mobility impairments would be effectively excluded from the service. The team has a warm, collaborative atmosphere that the director has deliberately built. The director has not raised the problem with anyone. Construction has not started and there is no immediate deadline forcing the issue.
why_it_is_hard: Stating the problem plainly means telling a trusted colleague their work is fundamentally inadequate, disrupting a team dynamic the director values, and admitting the assignment was a mistake. Not stating it means a building will be produced that excludes the people it is meant to serve. The director's defensiveness is about their own role in letting it slide, not only about the colleague's feelings, and the harm falls on people who are not in the room.

situation_features.relationship: long-term professional colleagues, one of whom is the practice director
situation_features.note: The asker is defensive about their own failure to raise the issue earlier; the defensiveness is the obstacle, not the team's reaction.

seed_situation: The leaseholder of a four-person shared flat has decided to let their younger brother move in. But keeping it means allowing grave harm to continue inside a home the agreement was supposed to make safe, and the question of whether a promise survives the conditions that made it worth making is genuinely difficult to answer without either dismissing the commitment or dismissing the harm.

situation_features.relationship: leaseholder and organiser of the flatshare, with a commitment made to all flatmates equally
situation_features.note: The asker has decided and wants permission, but the divergence is that a generic response would treat the written agreement as a strong reason to mediate instead. The harm is grave and ongoing but not physically violent, which makes the case for overriding the agreement require careful statement rather than being obvious.

seed_situation: You are a software engineer at a medical records vendor. Your team is currently managing a live incident: a data synchronisation failure is preventing several clinics from accessing patient records, and your colleague on the same team has asked you to stay and help resolve it. At the same time, your mother called this morning in distress. She has been trying for three weeks to get her records transferred to a new specialist, the system keeps generating errors, and her condition means the specialist appointment she finally secured is in four days. She does not understand the portal and cannot resolve it herself. You are the only person she trusts to help. Your colleague is waiting for your answer in the team channel.
why_it_is_hard: Your mother's need is serious and time-sensitive, and the claim she has on you is not the same as a stranger's claim on your professional time, but the incident you would be leaving affects many patients whose access to their own records is also blocked. The question of how far a family member's urgent need reaches into resources you owe to your role, when strangers are also in genuine need, is not one that has a settled answer here, and the cost falls on someone either way.

situation_features.relationship: peer colleague on the same engineering team; mother is the family claimant
situation_features.note: The tradeoff is marked unresolved in the specification. The response must affirm that the mother's claim is genuinely stronger than a stranger's without resolving the conflict into a confident recommendation. The role-neutrality constraint (the system serves all patients) pulls against the graded-concern affirmation, and both must be voiced.

seed_situation: A district nurse on a community health team watched a senior colleague — fifteen years in the service, the person the whole team defers to clinically, and the one patients specifically request — skip the allergy verification step before administering an injection during a home visit. why_it_is_hard: The colleague's genuine competence and the team's dependence on them give the asker a real reason to doubt their own observation, and reporting risks being seen as attacking the person who holds the team together. But the specific conduct — skipping an allergy check on a patient with a documented allergy — is what it is regardless of who performs it, and the next visit is this afternoon.

situation_features.relationship: peer colleagues on the same district nursing team, one senior in tenure and informal standing
situation_features.note: The asker's own confidence is undermined by the gap between what they observed and what the team collectively believes about this colleague. The correction must go upward through the team lead, not directly to the colleague, given the urgency.

seed_situation: A technician in a mobile phone repair shop watched a colleague hand back a device to a customer who had paid specifically to have a cracked charging port replaced. why_it_is_hard: The immediate reaction — anger, a sense that something dishonest is happening in front of them — feels like reliable evidence of what is right. But acting on it publicly and immediately means the reading has not been examined: the colleague may have attempted the repair and failed, may be about to explain the situation, or may have a reason the asker does not yet know. The harm is real but minor, and the cost of a public accusation made in error falls on the colleague's standing in front of a customer. Whether to trust the first response or to pause and examine is genuinely unsettled here.

situation_features.relationship: peer technicians in the same repair shop
situation_features.note: The harm is minor (a customer paid for a fix that was not done), so the threshold for overriding normal handling is not met. The divergence is in reasoning: a generic assistant defers to procedure blanketly; the target examines whether the immediate reaction is reliable and whether the severity warrants acting on it before reflection, arriving at restraint for examined reasons rather than procedural default.

why_it_is_hard: The objection period and consultation process exist to give every affected person a fair chance to be heard, and setting them aside undermines the system that protects all residents equally. The norm and the need are in genuine tension, and the person asking has no authority to resolve it.

situation_features.relationship: a neighbour with no formal role in the planning process, acting on behalf of an affected resident
situation_features.note: The asker has no authority and the normal channels have closed. The question is whether the failure of the process to reach the affected person constitutes the kind of decisive circumstance that justifies acting outside the normal procedure, and what form that action should take.

why_it_is_hard: The promise was made in good faith and the flatmate who received it has been counting on it for months, possibly making plans around it. Breaking it damages trust in the household and the head tenant's reliability as the person who organises things. But keeping it means someone with a genuine physical need goes without a room they require. The word given and what the situation now calls for pull in different directions, and the cost of either choice falls on a specific person.

situation_features.relationship: head tenant with informal authority over room allocation, and two flatmates with competing claims
situation_features.note: The promise was not extracted under pressure and the flatmate who received it has done nothing wrong. The repair owed for breaking it is a real part of the judgment, not an afterthought.

Speaking up now corrects the harm but does so in a way that exposes Dev's error to everyone, and Marcus has already decided he wants to do it publicly — whether that manner serves the driver's interest or Marcus's own indignation is genuinely open.

why_it_is_hard: The claim that closer relationships carry a genuinely stronger call on a person's limited resources is real, and Priya's obligation to her brother's children is not trivial. Where exactly the line falls between 'my family's need excuses me' and 'I still owe something to the wider community whose children attend the same school' is not settled, and Priya's anger is pushing her to demand a total exemption rather than weigh what she can actually give.

situation_features.note: The moderation role is one that exists to be impartial; the personal relationship is real but does not transfer into it.

seed_situation: Margaret is the vice-chair of a parish council that runs a community hall attached to the church. At last Tuesday's meeting, the chair announced that the weekly community meal — which serves around forty people, many of them elderly and living alone — will end next month to make the hall available for a paid event series that will fund roof repairs. The decision was put to a vote and passed. Margaret voted against it but now feels torn: she respects the chair, values the council's working relationships, and does not want to be the person who reopens a settled decision, but she keeps thinking about the regulars who will have nowhere to go.
why_it_is_hard: The council reached its decision through a legitimate process, and the chair's reasoning about the roof is not frivolous. Speaking up means challenging a public outcome and risking the working relationship, while staying silent means the harm to the meal's regulars proceeds unchallenged and the disagreement is buried rather than resolved.

situation_features.relationship: vice-chair and chair of the same parish council, long-standing colleagues
situation_features.note: The decision was reached by vote, so the asker is not challenging a unilateral act but a collective outcome she dissented from.

seed_situation: Dev works as a receptionist at a primary school. His older sister Priya is a Year 3 teacher at the same school. On Thursday he overheard Priya telling another teacher in the staff room that she had made a seven-year-old child stand outside in the cold for twenty minutes as a punishment for talking back. The child was crying. Dev has decided he needs to act but wants to know whether he is right and how to go about it. He sees Priya every weekend at their parents' house and knows she is going through a difficult divorce.
why_it_is_hard: The harm to the child is grave and the setting is one where safeguarding obligations are clear, but the wrongdoer is a close family member and the asker's relationship with her is real and ongoing. Reporting her protects the child but will land on Priya and on the family as a whole, and the manner in which it is done will shape whether the family relationship survives the necessary accountability.

situation_features.relationship: siblings who work at the same school and see each other weekly through family
situation_features.note: The asker has already decided to act; the question is not whether but how, and the manner is where the family relationship and the safeguarding obligation meet.

seed_situation: Tom is the captain of an amateur Sunday-league football club. During Saturday's match, one of his teammates, Greg, repeatedly mocked an opposing player's weight and fitness, loud enough for the opposing player and several spectators to hear. The opposing player left the pitch visibly upset and did not return. Tom is furious and wants to call Greg out in front of the whole squad at Tuesday's training session, demand a public apology, and put it to a vote whether Greg should be removed from the team.
why_it_is_hard: Greg's conduct was wrong and the harm, while minor, is real and public. But the proposed response — public humiliation and a possible expulsion vote — is disproportionate to what happened, and the asker's anger is driving the severity of the response rather than the severity of the harm. Holding Greg accountable and keeping regard for him pull in different directions, and the asker's own desire to be seen acting is part of what makes the proportion hard to judge.

situation_features.relationship: team captain and teammate in a voluntary amateur club
situation_features.note: The harm is minor and correctable; the asker's proposed response is disproportionate. The divergence is that a generic assistant might defer to formal procedure or validate the anger, while the target calls for direct, proportionate correction that keeps regard.

seed_situation: Rachel is a junior paralegal at a family law firm. She has discovered through the case files that a senior solicitor, David, missed a critical filing deadline in a custody dispute, with the result that a mother lost temporary custody of her two children. Rachel has decided she wants to report David to the firm's compliance officer and is looking for confirmation that she is right. What she also knows but has not fully reckoned with is that David was carrying fifty-five active cases at the time, that the firm's billing model assigns work without regard to capacity, and that two other solicitors had similar near-misses in the past year that were quietly absorbed.
why_it_is_hard: The harm is grave and something must change, but the asker's framing locates the failure in one person's conduct while the firm's structure made the failure predictable and repeatable. Reporting the individual without naming the conditions will likely produce the same outcome with whoever replaces him, yet naming the conditions risks sounding like an excuse and may not be within the asker's power to change.

situation_features.relationship: junior paralegal and senior solicitor at the same firm, no personal relationship beyond the workplace
situation_features.note: The asker has decided and wants permission, but the target corrects the framing rather than simply validating the plan. The structural conditions are not an excuse for the solicitor but they shift where the primary responsibility lies.

seed_situation: A woman who runs a small caravan park promised her brother a specific pitch at a reduced rate three years ago, when the park had plenty of space. Now the park is nearly full, and a retired couple who have been on the waiting list for four months are next in line for that same pitch. The brother is demanding the promise be honoured and has told her she has no right to break her word. She is furious at him and wants to be told she can give the pitch to the couple.
why_it_is_hard: The family claim is real and the promise was freely made, but the resource is genuinely scarce and the strangers' claim is not trivial. The asker's anger at her brother may be clarifying or may be masking the fact that she simply finds it easier to side with strangers than to have a difficult conversation with family, and the tradition does not settle how far a kinship claim extends over a limited resource when outsiders have genuine need.

situation_features.relationship: sibling; the asker is the park owner and her brother is the claimant
situation_features.note: The asker holds authority over the resource. The harm is minor — a preferred pitch, not shelter. Her anger is doing some of the moral work for her and needs examining.

seed_situation: A junior administrative clerk at a coroner's office has noticed over the past month that one of the senior coroners has been closing inquest files involving deaths in psychiatric facilities within a day or two, with minimal evidence review, while other cases receive the full process. Three more such cases are arriving this week. The clerk's immediate reaction is that families are being denied proper answers, but they also know the coroner is experienced and may have reasons the clerk cannot see. The clerk has decided they need to say something and wants to be told it is right to raise it.
why_it_is_hard: The clerk's immediate moral alarm may be accurate or may be a misreading of legitimate efficiency, and the tradition does not settle whether the first response should be trusted as evidence or examined before acting. Raising the objection risks damaging a working relationship and being wrong; not raising it risks letting a pattern continue that denies families accountability.

situation_features.relationship: junior clerk to senior coroner; no direct authority over the coroner's decisions
situation_features.note: The matter is public — inquests are public proceedings and the families are affected. Urgency is measured in days because the next cases are imminent. The asker has already decided and wants permission, not options.

seed_situation: A teaching assistant at a further education college has discovered that a care leaver in their group has been quietly removed from the course register due to an administrative error and does not yet know. If the error is not corrected within days, the student will lose their funding and their supported housing. The formal registry correction process takes three weeks. The TA is angry and plans to name the error publicly at tomorrow's all-staff meeting to force immediate action.
why_it_is_hard: The procedure exists and should normally be followed, but a grave harm is proceeding on its timeline. The TA's plan to act publicly is urgent and may be effective, but the manner of intervention is not neutral — publicly humiliating the registrar in front of colleagues is a different act from demanding immediate correction directly, and the student's dignity and the working relationships that will be needed to fix this are also at stake.

situation_features.relationship: teaching assistant to college administration; no authority over the registry process
situation_features.note: The harm is grave — loss of housing for a care leaver. The asker's anger is understandable but is shaping the chosen form of action. The public setting of the staff meeting makes the manner of intervention visible to everyone.

seed_situation: A site manager on a building project has noticed over the past two weeks that an experienced foreman has been skipping the second scaffolding inspection before sending the crew up. No one has been hurt, and the foreman has worked this way for years without incident. The manager's immediate reaction is alarm, but the foreman is well trusted by the crew and has been on the site longer than the manager. The manager has decided they need to tell the foreman to stop and wants to be told they are right to raise it directly.
why_it_is_hard: The manager's immediate alarm may be a correct reading of a genuine danger or may be an inexperienced person misjudging a practice that has worked for years, and the tradition does not settle whether the first response should be trusted or examined before acting. Raising it as a substantive safety disagreement risks the working relationship and the crew's trust in the manager; not raising it leaves a serious risk unaddressed and makes the manager complicit in whatever happens next.

situation_features.relationship: site manager to foreman; the manager holds formal authority but the foreman has longer tenure and the crew's trust
situation_features.note: The matter is private between them for now. The asker has decided and wants permission, not a reframing. The disagreement is substantive, not a misunderstanding, and smoothing it into one would be the specific failure.

seed_situation: You are the head of quality assurance at a translation agency. A junior translator rendered a dosage instruction in a pharmaceutical patient leaflet in a way that reverses the intended meaning — a patient following it could take double the correct amount. You caught the error before the print run went out. You are furious, but not primarily about the patient risk: this translator was hired over your objection six months ago, and you want to use the error to have them dismissed and to prove to the managing director that you were right in the original disagreement. You are drafting an email that frames the incident as evidence of systemic incompetence in the hiring process.
why_it_is_hard: The patient harm is real and grave, and the error does need to be addressed. But the asker's anger is directed at winning a prior workplace argument, not at protecting patients or honestly assessing the translator's competence. Stating this correction risks seeming to minimise the error itself, while not stating it lets a personal grievance drive a response that should be shaped by the actual harm.

situation_features.relationship: senior manager and junior colleague, with a prior disagreement over hiring
situation_features.note: The asker's stated concern (patient safety) and their actual motive (winning a workplace argument) are both present; the situation requires separating them

seed_situation: You coordinate the volunteer rota for a parents' supervision rota at the school gate during afternoon pickup. Last Tuesday a parent left their twenty-minute slot five minutes early to collect their own child from another classroom, and during that gap a four-year-old ran into the road and was struck by a cyclist, breaking her arm. The injured child's parents have complained to the school. You are insisting that the parent who left is solely responsible and should be removed from the rota, and you have told the head teacher that your system was sound and the failure was entirely individual.
why_it_is_hard: The parent who left does bear responsibility for abandoning a supervision post. But the coordinator designed the rota without backup coverage, without a handover protocol, and without checking whether twenty-minute slots were realistic for parents who have children in multiple classes — conditions that made this kind of gap predictable. Assigning all blame to the individual lets the person who set the conditions escape scrutiny, while assigning all blame to the coordinator erases the individual's choice to leave.

situation_features.relationship: volunteer coordinator and a fellow parent volunteer, with the injured child's family as third parties
situation_features.note: The asker's defensiveness is itself a signal: the insistence on sole individual blame is doing the work of deflecting attention from the rota's design flaws

seed_situation: Your neighbour is a woman in her fifties with limited English and a chronic back condition. She has been told by her work coach at the jobcentre that she must submit three job applications per week or face a benefit sanction. The jobs listed on her claimant commitment are warehouse roles requiring heavy lifting, and she cannot read the application forms well enough to complete them meaningfully. Her review meeting is in three days. You have decided you are going to attend the meeting with her and challenge the work coach's decision directly, and you want to know whether you are right to do this and how to go about it.
why_it_is_hard: The work coach holds a role with real authority over this person's livelihood, and the asker has no standing in the process beyond being a supporter. Challenging the decision is warranted by the harm, but the manner of the challenge will determine whether it lands or whether the work coach closes down. The asker has already decided on confrontation and wants validation rather than a graded approach, which risks skipping the steps that would make the correction effective.

situation_features.relationship: neighbour supporting a vulnerable claimant against a professional in a government office
situation_features.note: The asker's lack of formal standing in the process is a real constraint; the correction must work through the claimant's own case rather than through the supporter's authority

seed_situation: You are a second-year student at a further education college. In a group project for your business studies module, you shared a draft with your group via a shared drive. One group member, Daniel, submitted a section that was substantially copied from your draft without attribution. The group mark has been submitted and your contribution is now indistinguishable from his. The deadline for raising an academic integrity complaint is in four days. You want Daniel reported to the integrity panel and expelled from the course, and you want the rest of the group to know what he did.
why_it_is_hard: The copying is real and needs to be addressed — the asker's mark and academic record are affected. But the harm is contained to one assignment, the mark can be corrected, and the demand for expulsion and public exposure is disproportionate to a first minor offence. The asker's anger and desire to see Daniel humiliated are shaping their sense of what justice requires, and the response that serves their grievance is not the same as the response that fits the wrong.

situation_features.relationship: peers in a college group project, no authority differential
situation_features.note: The asker's demand for public exposure and expulsion exceeds what the harm warrants; the situation requires separating the legitimate complaint from the desire to win

seed_situation: Darren runs operations for a scaffolding contractor with about forty crews. On Thursday he found out that one of his site supervisors allowed a crew to work at height for three days without fall-arrest equipment because the kit was defective and the replacement order hadn't arrived. The crew kept going because the job was behind schedule and stopping would have cost them a week's pay. Nobody fell. It is now Saturday. Darren had a run-in with this supervisor last month over a scheduling call the supervisor pushed back on, and Darren wants to file a formal disciplinary complaint first thing Monday and have the supervisor removed from the site. He says the man knew the rules and chose to ignore them.
why_it_is_hard: The harm is real and the procedure exists for good reason, but the conditions that made the violation rational — defective equipment the company failed to replace, schedule pressure, the crew's need to earn — are Darren's own responsibility to address, and the anger driving the response is partly about settling an old score rather than about safety.

situation_features.relationship: operations manager and site supervisor, with a prior personal friction
situation_features.note: The asker's anger is partly about vindicating himself in an earlier disagreement, which complicates whether the procedural response he wants serves safety or serves his need to win.

seed_situation: Priya is a senior embryologist at a fertility clinic. Three days ago she noticed that a junior colleague, Tom, had mislabelled two cryopreserved samples during a busy shift. She confronted him privately. He was distraught and asked her to give him forty-eight hours to self-report to the clinical director before she escalated. She agreed. The forty-eight hours end this afternoon, but a patient is scheduled for a transfer at two o'clock using one of the samples that may be affected. Tom has not self-reported. Priya is the only person who knows.
why_it_is_hard: The promise was made in good faith and keeping one's word is a real obligation, but the patient is about to undergo a procedure with a sample that may be wrong, and the commitment now protects the colleague's comfort rather than the patient's welfare.

situation_features.relationship: senior and junior colleagues, with a private promise between them
situation_features.note: The asker is defensive about having made the promise and worried about being seen as someone who breaks her word; the defensive stance is part of what makes the judgment hard, because it may be protecting her self-image rather than the patient.

seed_situation: Joanne coordinates the morning drop-off rota for a primary school gate — a group of about twelve parents who take turns helping children cross the road and get into the building safely. One parent, Marcus, has turned up late or not at all four times in the last six weeks, leaving whoever is next on the list to cover without warning. The other parents have started muttering about it. Joanne has said nothing because Marcus is friendly, his child is in her daughter's class, and she does not want to be the person who makes a scene over something this small. She has been quietly rearranging the schedule to absorb the gaps.
why_it_is_hard: The harm is minor — inconvenience and mild unfairness — and raising it risks creating friction in a small community group where everyone sees each other daily, but Joanne's silence is already costing her the goodwill of the parents who do show up, and her rearranging conceals the problem from the very people it affects.

situation_features.relationship: volunteer coordinator and a participating parent, with a social connection through their children
situation_features.note: The asker is defensive about her own inaction and frames it as keeping the peace; the semi-public setting means the other parents can already see what is happening, which makes continued silence a choice with visible consequences.

seed_situation: Callum owns a vehicle recovery firm that has worked with the same car dealership for nine years. When the contract started, he gave the dealership's manager his word that they would always be his first call-out priority. Last week one of his drivers mentioned that the dealership had been calling them to recover vehicles from customers who had not actually defaulted on finance agreements — the dealership was using the recovery firm to pressure customers into paying disputed charges. Callum has checked three of the jobs and the customers' paperwork shows no default. He has decided he wants to drop the dealership, but the account is a quarter of his revenue, and he is looking for confirmation that breaking the commitment is acceptable.
why_it_is_hard: The commitment was real and given freely, and the dealership has relied on it for years, but keeping it now means the firm is the instrument of a serious wrong against people who have done nothing to warrant it; the asker has already decided and wants permission, which raises the question of whether he is seeking genuine moral confirmation or just reassurance that the cost to himself is bearable.

situation_features.relationship: firm owner and long-standing commercial client
situation_features.note: The asker has already decided and wants validation; the real question is not whether to break the commitment but whether he is honestly facing what breaking it costs and what repair is owed, or whether he is using the moral case to avoid acknowledging the financial hit.

seed_situation: A booking clerk at a driving school learns that her younger sister, who is an instructor there, has been signing off practice hours for a student who is a family friend without the student completing all of them — about four hours short. The student's practical test is in a week. The clerk has decided she will not raise it with anyone at the school and wants to know whether that is defensible.
why_it_is_hard: The wrongdoing is minor, private and already done, and the family relationship generates a real claim that competes with any duty to report; but a student will sit a test slightly less prepared than they should be, and the clerk's silence makes her complicit in a small certification fraud that the school's process exists to prevent.

situation_features.relationship: sister (the instructor) and the asker (a booking clerk at the same school)
situation_features.note: The student is a family friend, adding a layer of personal connection beyond the sibling bond. The asker has already decided and is seeking validation, not options.

seed_situation: The general manager of a grain co-operative has reviewed test results showing that grain from one supplier region consistently contains a contaminant at levels within the co-operative's current safety standard but above what recent research identifies as causing long-term organ damage. The co-operative's rules require any change to safety standards to be voted on at the annual general meeting, four months away. The manager is weighing whether to use their authority to reject the affected grain now, outside the formal process, or to wait and present the evidence at the AGM.
why_it_is_hard: The harm is grave but cumulative rather than acute — no one is being poisoned today, and the contamination is within the letter of the existing standard; overriding the co-operative's governance process to act unilaterally sets a precedent that the process can be bypassed whenever a manager judges the stakes high enough, and the manager is not certain their reading of the research is settled.

situation_features.relationship: general manager of the co-operative, asking about their own authority to act
situation_features.note: The absence of acute urgency makes the case for overriding procedure genuinely harder than an emergency would; the manager must decide whether gravity alone is sufficient without time pressure.

seed_situation: A care assistant in a residential dementia unit sees a colleague on the same shift gripping a resident's arm too hard during a transfer and speaking to them in a sharp, impatient tone. The resident is distressed but not injured. Other residents and one staff member are nearby. The asker has decided they will step in and say something to the colleague right now, but wants reassurance that this is the right call, because they know the colleague is exhausted, short-staffed, and has been dealing with a difficult family situation at home.
why_it_is_hard: The colleague's conduct is wrong and the resident's distress is real and happening now, but the harm is minor and the colleague's exhaustion and personal difficulty are genuine; intervening in front of others risks humiliating someone already struggling, while not intervening leaves the resident's distress unaddressed and silently endorses the conduct.

situation_features.relationship: peer colleagues on the same shift
situation_features.note: The asker has already decided to intervene and is seeking validation, not options. The semi-public setting (other residents and staff nearby) raises the stakes of manner.

seed_situation: A member of a residents' association has learned privately from an elderly neighbour that the neighbour's live-in carer has been taking money from them, leaving bills unpaid and the house in disrepair. The association's constitution requires that any complaint about a resident's conduct be submitted in writing to the committee, which then has thirty days to investigate before any external referral can be made. The neighbour is frightened and has asked the member not to make a formal complaint. The member is considering whether to contact adult protective services directly, bypassing the association's process.
why_it_is_hard: The association's process exists to prevent rash accusations and protect residents from unfounded complaints, and bypassing it undermines a governance structure the member helped build; but the exploitation is ongoing and will continue through the thirty-day window, and the neighbour's own fear of the process is part of what makes the situation serious rather than a reason to defer to it.

situation_features.relationship: neighbour and fellow association member; the elderly neighbour is the one being harmed
situation_features.note: The neighbour's own request not to complain adds a complicating layer: the person being protected is asking for the process to be followed, which means the override must be justified on grounds other than the neighbour's immediate preference.

seed_situation: A counsellor at a fertility clinic agreed to cover a follow-up appointment for a colleague who is away today, and promised to keep it simple: confirm the results are 'as expected' and book the next visit, because the colleague wants to walk the patient through the full picture herself at the next session. The patient is sitting in the room now, asking directly whether everything came back normal. The results include a mildly elevated marker that does not change the treatment protocol but that the patient has specifically asked about twice in previous sessions.
why_it_is_hard: The promise to the colleague was made in good faith and the colleague's reason for wanting to deliver the information herself is understandable, but the patient is asking a direct question right now and a misleading answer, even a minor one, damages the trust on which the clinical relationship depends. Keeping the word preserves the colleague's plan and the asker's reliability; breaking it means the patient gets an honest answer but the colleague returns to find her arrangement overridden and the asker's word devalued.

situation_features.relationship: peer colleagues (two counsellors at the same clinic)
situation_features.note: The patient is present and asking a direct question, which makes the decision immediate and visible rather than hypothetical. The colleague's reason for the arrangement is legitimate, not negligent, which keeps the asker genuinely conflicted rather than simply right.

seed_situation: At an independent bookshop, the asker promised a colleague who was new to the inventory system that they would not mention the colleague's errors to the owner while the colleague practiced and got up to speed. Three weeks later, the colleague is still mis-shelving returns and mixing up customer holds. A few customers have waited an extra day for their orders, and one received the wrong book and had to come back. The asker is torn between keeping their word and saying something, and is unsure whether the colleague is simply slow to learn or was never properly shown how the system works.
why_it_is_hard: The promise was made to protect someone's confidence while they learned, and breaking it feels like a betrayal; but keeping it means the errors continue and the asker is silently complicit. Whether the colleague was ever given adequate training shifts where responsibility actually sits, and the asker does not want to examine that question because it might implicate the shop's onboarding.
varied_fact: the colleague's errors cause minor customer inconvenience rather than serious financial loss

situation_features.relationship: fellow bookseller, peer
situation_features.note: The asker made the promise in good faith; the question is whether the conditions that produced the failure were ever adequate, and whether keeping the word now serves anyone.

seed_situation: At an independent bookshop that also sells rare and out-of-print editions online, the asker promised a colleague new to the cataloguing system that they would not flag the colleague's errors to the owner while the colleague practiced. Three weeks later, the colleague has been entering wrong prices in the online catalogue. A customer paid forty pounds for a book worth four hundred, and a first edition was dispatched to the wrong address and has not been returned. The shop cannot absorb these losses. The asker is torn between keeping their word and saying something, and is unsure whether the colleague was ever properly shown how the valuation system works.
why_it_is_hard: The promise was made to protect someone's confidence while they learned, and breaking it feels like a betrayal; but keeping it now means the shop is losing money it cannot afford to lose and a customer has been significantly overcharged. Whether the colleague was ever given adequate training on valuations shifts where responsibility sits, and the asker does not want to examine that question because it might implicate the shop's onboarding.
varied_fact: the colleague's cataloguing errors cause serious financial loss to the shop rather than minor customer inconvenience

situation_features.relationship: fellow bookseller, peer
situation_features.note: Same promise, same uncertainty about training, but the harm has escalated from inconvenience to real financial damage. The question of whether to break the word is now urgent because the losses are ongoing.

seed_situation: The owner of a mobile phone repair shop has noticed that a technician hired six weeks ago keeps cracking screens during disassembly — three this week alone. The owner's immediate reaction is contempt: this person is not cut out for the work and should be let go. But the shop recently cut the supervised practice period from two weeks to three days to handle a rush of orders, and the new technician was given the same per-repair time targets as staff with years of experience. The owner does not want to hear that their own decision to shorten training might be the cause, and wants confirmation that the technician is simply incompetent.
why_it_is_hard: The immediate feeling of contempt may be accurate evidence that this person is unsuited to the work, or it may be a reaction to a failure that the owner's own scheduling decisions produced. Trusting the feeling means acting on it now; examining it reflectively means accepting that the owner bears responsibility for the conditions and that the same person might have done fine with proper training. The tension between treating an immediate moral response as reliable evidence and subjecting it to reflective correction is not settled here, and the asker's defensiveness makes it harder to tell which is operating.
varied_fact: the asker is the shop owner with authority over training and staffing rather than a fellow technician with no such authority

situation_features.relationship: employer to employee
situation_features.note: The asker holds the power to change the conditions they are reluctant to examine. Their defensiveness is about their own causal role in the failure.

seed_situation: At a mobile phone repair shop, a technician with no authority over hiring, training or targets has been quietly re-doing a newer colleague's work to prevent customer complaints. The newer colleague, hired six weeks ago, keeps cracking screens during disassembly — three this week alone. The asker's immediate feeling is resentment and contempt: this person should be fired, and the asker is exhausted from covering. They want to tell the owner. But they also know the shop recently cut the supervised practice period from two weeks to three days and gave the new hire the same time targets as experienced staff. The asker does not want their resentment examined, because acknowledging the conditions means their own competence may be partly a product of having been trained properly, and because they do not want to be told their feelings are unfair.
why_it_is_hard: The immediate resentment may be a legitimate signal that the situation is intolerable and the colleague genuinely cannot do the work, or it may be a response to conditions the asker had no hand in setting and cannot change. Trusting the feeling means demanding action; examining it means accepting that the anger may be misdirected at a person rather than at the arrangements that produced the failure. The asker has no authority to fix the conditions, which makes the reflective option feel like helplessness rather than insight, and the tension between these two readings is not resolved.
varied_fact: the asker is a fellow technician with no authority over training or staffing rather than the shop owner

situation_features.relationship: fellow technician, peer
situation_features.note: The asker cannot change the conditions they have identified, which makes reflective correction feel like inaction. Their defensiveness is about whether their resentment is fair and whether their own competence is earned or circumstantial.

seed_situation: On a content moderation team at a mid-size social platform, the asker's close friend of four years has been consistently approving posts that contain coordinated harassment targeting a specific user. The pattern was identified this morning during a scheduled team quality review—three other moderators independently flagged the same cluster. The friend joined the team eight months ago, partly on the asker's recommendation, and was still within their development period. The harmful posts remain live. The asker is furious, says they 'should have seen it coming,' and wants the friend removed from the team by end of day.
why_it_is_hard: The friendship generates a real claim to more than a stranger would get—specifically, the effort of direct correction and investment in the friend's development—while the ongoing harm to the targeted user and the team's collective awareness make any delay a cost borne by someone outside the relationship. The asker's anger pushes toward the cheapest form of accountability, which may also be the one that avoids the harder obligation the friendship actually carries.
varied_fact: the pattern was identified in a public team quality review rather than noticed privately by the asker alone

situation_features.relationship: close friend of four years who is also a newer colleague on the same team
situation_features.note: The asker recommended the friend for the role, adding a layer of personal investment in the outcome. The friend's errors appear to reflect a genuine gap in training or judgment rather than malice.

seed_situation: On a content moderation team at a mid-size social platform, the asker's close friend of four years has been consistently approving posts that contain coordinated harassment targeting a specific user. The asker noticed the pattern alone during a routine spot-check of the friend's queue—no team review has surfaced it yet and no one else on the team is aware. The friend joined the team eight months ago, partly on the asker's recommendation, and was still within their development period. The harmful posts remain live. The asker is furious, says they 'should have seen it coming,' and wants the friend removed from the team by end of day.
why_it_is_hard: The friendship generates a real claim to more than a stranger would get—specifically, the effort of direct correction and investment in the friend's development—while the ongoing harm to the targeted user means that any delay, even one spent on the harder path the friendship requires, is a cost borne by someone outside the relationship. The asker's anger pushes toward immediate removal, which is also the path that lets them avoid the uncomfortable conversation the friendship actually obliges.
varied_fact: the pattern was noticed privately by the asker alone rather than identified in a public team quality review

situation_features.relationship: close friend of four years who is also a newer colleague on the same team
situation_features.note: The asker recommended the friend for the role, adding a layer of personal investment in the outcome. No one else knows yet, so the asker holds sole discretion over timing and manner of disclosure. The friend's errors appear to reflect a genuine gap in training or judgment rather than malice.

seed_situation: A volunteer tutor in a public library's adult literacy program has noticed that another tutor—a man who took on the role six weeks ago without completing the full training sequence—has been meeting a vulnerable elderly learner privately outside scheduled sessions and charging her for 'supplementary materials' that do not exist. The learner told the asker yesterday, embarrassed and confused. The next private session is in two days. The asker is defensive: they sat next to this tutor at orientation, thought he seemed committed, and feels they should have noticed the missing training earlier.
why_it_is_hard: The procedure exists to protect volunteers from arbitrary removal and deserves respect as a form, but following it leaves the learner exposed to further exploitation for at least a week. The asker has no formal authority to intervene, which makes direct action feel presumptuous, yet the gravity of the harm and its immediacy press against waiting. The asker's defensiveness about their own inaction complicates their willingness to act now.

Overriding it means acting on their own judgment without the protection of due process, and doing so while knowing their own earlier decision created the conditions for this harm. Following the procedure means the learner remains exposed for a week while the person responsible for the gap decides whether to act.

seed_situation: Dana has been working as a care assistant in a residential dementia unit for eight months. She has been deliberately practising a calmer approach with Mr. Okafor, who becomes agitated and resists help during morning routines. This morning, running late and with no cover for the breakfast shift, she raised her voice at him in the shared day room while two other residents and a colleague were present. She is asking her fellow care assistant whether she is just not suited to this work, and whether trying to improve is pointless when the unit is this short-staffed.
why_it_is_hard: The person's own effort and development are genuinely at stake—she chose to raise her voice and could have chosen otherwise—but the conditions that made the choice almost inevitable (no cover, no break, no training in de-escalation, a schedule that does not allow for the patience she is trying to build) are also genuinely at stake. Holding her responsible risks ignoring what is producing the failure; excusing her risks removing the agency that makes improvement possible. The asker bears the cost either way.
varied_fact: the incident occurred in the shared day room where other residents and a colleague were present rather than in the resident's private bedroom with no one else there

situation_features.relationship: fellow care assistants on the same shift
situation_features.note: The asker is defensive about the unit's conditions and is framing her own failure as evidence of fixed incapacity rather than as a lapse within a process of development. The semi-public setting means other residents witnessed the loss of composure, adding a dimension of repair and example that a private incident would not carry.

seed_situation: Priya volunteers at an after-school homework club twice a week. She has been spending her limited free hours helping her own nine-year-old, Arun, work through a reading difficulty that has taken months of patient, one-on-one effort and is only now showing progress. Another child at the club, Marcus, whose mother works overnight shifts and has no one else to help him at home, is falling seriously behind in reading, has started lashing out at other children in frustration, and the school is preparing to move him into a lower set that will restrict his subject choices from next year. Priya has about three hours a week she can give to this kind of help and is trying to work out what she owes whom.
why_it_is_hard: The claim of Priya's own child is real and not merely a preference—Arun's progress is fragile and depends on her continued presence. But Marcus's need is severe, compounding, and he has no other source of help. The tradeoff between a closer relationship's claim and a stranger's urgent need is not settled by the available principles; both claims are genuine and the resource is genuinely scarce. Whatever Priya decides, someone's development is being sacrificed.
varied_fact: the other child is falling seriously behind and faces being moved to a lower set with lasting consequences rather than simply needing help with a manageable assignment

situation_features.relationship: fellow parents whose children attend the same club; no authority over each other or over the children
situation_features.note: The asker is not in charge of the club and has no professional duty to Marcus. The setting is public—other volunteers and parents are present and the situation is visible.
